summary: Discovery focused on p95 latency targets and throughput for streaming chat and batch token workloads. Customer is evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs private (VPC) with strict p95 targets around 200-300ms for interactive triage flows and higher throughput for background scoring. Action items: benchmark run, pricing, security docs.
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya, I'm the AE on the Redwood side. We have Daniel, our SE, and Carlos from solutions. Quick intros?
[00:08] Dr. Sarah Lee: Hi, Sarah here, CTO at Lumina Health. We've got Priya (ML) and Mark (infra) and Alex from product. Thanks for doing this.
[00:15] Maya Patel: Of course. Goal for today is to understand your latency and throughput targets, concurrency, streaming needs, and where you are on hosted/dedicated/private decisions. We'll also capture success criteria and next steps.
[00:28] Priya Sharma: I'll jump in — our main use case is a triage chat that clinicians use. It's interactive, streaming preferred, and we need p95 sub-300ms for the token delivery during a live session ideally. For end-to-end turn latency p95 we were targeting ~400ms but token streaming really helps perceived latency.
[00:45] Mark Johnson: On infra side we care about concurrency. Typical day traffic: about 800 concurrent active sessions during peak, average message length ~80 tokens. Background jobs for reranking/embeddings hit batch throughput — around 200 qps of 512-token sequences.
[01:05] Daniel Kim: Got it. A couple clarifying Qs: when you say p95 sub-300ms for token delivery, is that per token emit or user-visible turn p95?
[01:12] Priya Sharma: Per token while streaming is the main metric, so the initial token should be quick and subsequent tokens arrival cadence should be steady — we care about token/sec and jitter too. For full-turn p95 we can tolerate up to 800ms depending on complexity.
[01:24] Maya Patel: Thanks. For benchmarking we usually look at 90/95/99 latencies, steady-state throughput, and concurrency. On hosted, we publish profiles for open models — but given your PII and PHI we know you're leaning toward either Dedicated or Private VPC. Is that correct?
[01:38] Dr. Sarah Lee: Yes, data residency and audit logs are a must. SOC 2, KMS, and SSO. We want the control plane options as well.
[01:45] Carlos Rivera: We support a private control plane and on-prem installs. For Dedicated, you get reserved GPU pools with KMS integration and audit logs. For private, you can run our control plane in your VPC.
[01:56] Alex Wu: Latency-wise, are there differences between hosted and dedicated for similar hardware?
[02:02] Daniel Kim: Good Q. If the hardware is the same, Dedicated and Hosted have comparable runtime; differences come from noisy neighbors on shared pools and routing overhead. Dedicated gives you reserved capacity so you'll hit target p95 more reliably. Private can be tuned further since network topology is under your control.
[02:19] Mark Johnson: We're evaluating A100 vs H100 nodes. Any guidance on token/sec for each?
[02:25] Daniel Kim: Broadly, H100 tends to give ~1.5-2x inference throughput for transformer decoding workloads depending on quantization and sequence lengths. For example, for a 13B model at 512 seq running with optimized kernels, you might see ~300-600 tokens/sec on A100 and ~600-1000 tokens/sec on H100 per GPU under continuous decoding. But exact numbers depend on batching, KV cache warm-hot rates, and kernel fusion.
[02:47] Priya Sharma: We're using a 34B open model variant for quality. Does that change the numbers?
[02:52] Daniel Kim: 34B will reduce tokens/sec by a factor; maybe 3-5x slower than 13B depending on quant. We're big on offering quantization-friendly paths and we can recommend int8/4-bit profiles that preserve quality while improving throughput. For streaming, effective tokens/sec also depends on beam width and sampling temperature.
[03:10] Maya Patel: Can you share your target p95 again?
[03:13] Priya Sharma: Per token p95 ideally <300ms and full-turn p95 <800ms at 800 concurrent sessions. Also for reranking batch work we want 200 qps at 512 tokens with p95 <1.2s.
[03:26] Daniel Kim: Those are challenging but plausible. For Dedicated we would size GPU pool to meet concurrency and apply intelligent batching for background jobs. For streaming, continuous-mode batching and small max batch windows keep latency low.
[03:38] Mark Johnson: A few more infra details — we run in AWS us-east-1, use VPC peering, all traffic must go through our transit gateway, and we require customer-managed KMS. Is that supported?
[03:50] Carlos Rivera: Yes, VPC deployments can use your KMS and private routing. For Dedicated we can set up peering and private IPs, and we support HSM/KMS integrations.
[03:59] Alex Wu: On reliability — if one GPU node is overloaded, what's the fallback?
[04:04] Daniel Kim: We have smart routing: requests can be routed to other capacity tiers or model variants. You can configure fallback to smaller models or lower-quality quantized variants. Also we have automatic retries and graceful degradation policies.
[04:18] Priya Sharma: For our benchmarking we want to emulate real clinician sessions which are bursty, and measure p95 across bursts. Can Redwood's benchmark harness replay our prompt traces?
[04:27] Daniel Kim: Yes, we can ingest your trace, including per-message timestamps and simulate session-level concurrency, streaming behavior and cold vs warm KV cache scenarios. We'll run both cold-start and warm path tests.
[04:38] Dr. Sarah Lee: Cost is also a factor. If Dedicated is cheaper per token at our volume, that might push us that way but we need SLA.
[04:46] Maya Patel: For pricing we'll show Hosted vs Dedicated commit tiers and typical unit economics after batching and caching. Redwood Optimize will give suggestions that often cut cost by 20-40% depending on workload.
[04:58] Mark Johnson: Regarding metrics — we need end-to-end p95 (including network), and server-side p95 (decode time). Can we export traces to our observability stack?
[05:08] Carlos Rivera: Yes, we have tracing hooks and per-route dashboards. You can push traces to your system via OTLP and we can provide token-level cost and latency breakdown.
[05:18] Priya Sharma: About tokenization — we have mixed-length messages. Will batching hurt short-turn latency?
[05:24] Daniel Kim: We use latency-aware batching. For short messages we cap the batch window and prefer immediate dispatch; for background batch jobs we maximize batch sizes. You can tune policies by route.
[05:35] Alex Wu: Any guidance on concurrency per GPU for streaming sessions?
[05:39] Daniel Kim: Concurrency per GPU varies by model size. For a 13B on H100, we've seen ~80-150 concurrent streaming sessions per GPU with steady token emission if sessions average short messages. For 34B that number drops — you might be in the 20-50 concurrent sessions range. Again, with quantization and optimized kernels you can push concurrency up.
[05:58] Priya Sharma: We also need to measure jitter and per-token p95 in ms distribution. Can you produce percentile histograms from the benchmark?
[06:05] Daniel Kim: Absolutely — we produce p50/p90/p95/p99 distributions and token-level inter-arrival jitter. We'll include warm vs cold cache comparisons and the effects of continuous batching.
[06:16] Dr. Sarah Lee: Security note — we need audit logs for data access and model versions used for an inference.
[06:22] Carlos Rivera: Audit logs are supported; we can log model SHA, version, request IDs and redacted inputs if required.
[06:28] Mark Johnson: One concern — when you say token/sec numbers, do those include tokemization overhead and network?
[06:34] Daniel Kim: Good callout. Our internal token/sec is decode-only server-side. For end-to-end you add tokenization, network RTT, and client-side latency. In benchmarks we can measure both server decode throughput and end-to-end user-visible throughput with your environment included.
[06:50] Priya Sharma: For our POC we want a trial Dedicated cluster with H100s, run a 1-hour simulated workload with our traces, and then decide between Dedicated or Private. Does Redwood provide short trials?
[06:59] Maya Patel: Yes, we can provision a time-limited Dedicated trial cluster for benchmarking. We'll present sizing guidance and pricing options after the test.
[07:07] Alex Wu: How do you measure streaming perceived latency? We care about first-byte vs last-byte delivery.
[07:12] Daniel Kim: We measure first-token latency (time from request to first token), per-token inter-arrival percentiles, and full-turn latency. For streaming we also look at initial response time and steady-state token rate.
[07:24] Priya Sharma: Any network optimizations? We have clinicians in-office and remote; WAN can add 50-150ms.
[07:30] Daniel Kim: We recommend edge routing plus regional endpoints to minimize RTT. For Private you can colocate models in your VPC to avoid public internet hops.
[07:38] Dr. Sarah Lee: Let's talk tolerance — if p95 spikes during bursts, what's the mitigation?
[07:43] Carlos Rivera: Autoscaling policies, burst capacity and fallback to smaller model variants are typical mitigations. Also pre-warming capacity and prefix caching help.
[07:53] Priya Sharma: On token budgets: our UI expects streaming tokens at ~20 tokens/sec. If the model is slower we'll see stuttering.
[07:59] Daniel Kim: Correct. In benchmarks we'll measure tokens/sec and per-token variance.
[08:05] Mark Johnson: For the background reranking jobs, do you do batching across customers? We need isolation for PHI.
[08:12] Carlos Rivera: For Dedicated, batching is within your reserved capacity and doesn't mix customers. Shared hosted pools might share batching across tenants unless you choose Dedicated or Private.
[08:22] Priya Sharma: Ok. For the benchmark we want these scenarios: 1) Streaming interactive sessions at 800 concurrency using 34B quantized model, 2) Batch reranking 200 qps at 512 tokens, 3) Cold-start path with empty KV cache for first 5 minutes of test.
[08:37] Daniel Kim: We'll configure those three scenarios. Also recommend toggling temperature and sampling to measure worst-case emission patterns.
[08:46] Maya Patel: I'll document those scenarios as the test plan.
[08:49] Dr. Sarah Lee: How long does it take to spin a Dedicated trial with H100?
[08:53] Carlos Rivera: Typically 48-72 hours to provision in our Dedicated pool depending on region and inventory. For Private on-prem it's longer.
[08:59] Alex Wu: What about cost estimate for a week-long test?
[09:03] Maya Patel: We'll give an estimate; expect trial discounts but we'll show standard committed pricing for comparison.
[09:10] Priya Sharma: One technical question: how do you handle long context windows and KV cache memory pressure? We do multi-turn conversations with context up to 8k tokens.
[09:19] Daniel Kim: We manage KV cache with eviction policies and efficient memory layouts. For extremely long contexts we offload cold KV pages to host memory and keep hot KV on GPU. We'll show memory vs latency tradeoffs in the test results.
[09:33] Mark Johnson: For telemetry, can we get token-level cost mapping to endpoints?
[09:38] Carlos Rivera: Yes, our console breaks down cost per token by route/model and by token type. It helps you find hot prompts.
[09:45] Priya Sharma: About quantization — if we use int8 optimizations, do we risk hallucination increase?
[09:51] Daniel Kim: There's a tradeoff. We have validated quantization profiles per model to minimize quality regression. Redwood Optimize will run evals on your prompt set to measure regressions and recommend settings.
[10:04] Dr. Sarah Lee: Great. Any compliance red flags for healthcare PHI?
[10:09] Carlos Rivera: We support HIPAA controls in private deployments and can sign BAA for Dedicated/private. SOC 2 reports and audit logs provided. We'll share the compliance packet.
[10:18] Maya Patel: Quick recap and next steps?
[10:21] Priya Sharma: Send the benchmark harness and trial cluster, we'll provide traces and prompt sets.
[10:25] Maya Patel: Action items: Daniel will prepare the test plan and harness, Maya will send pricing and security docs, Priya will share traces and sample prompts. Schedule follow-up for week of 11/4 for results and deeper streaming deep-dive.
[10:38] Dr. Sarah Lee: Sounds good. A couple of final quick Qs: do you support gRPC streaming and websocket?
[10:44] Daniel Kim: Yes to both; we recommend gRPC for lower overhead and precision measurement.
[10:49] Alex Wu: Who will be our primary Redwood contacts?
[10:52] Maya Patel: I'll be your AE, Daniel will run the benchmarks, and Carlos will help with dedicated provisioning.
[10:58] Mark Johnson: Anything else we should be aware of during the trial?
[11:02] Carlos Rivera: Make sure you provide representative auth flows and network configs so we can simulate your real path.
[11:08] Priya Sharma: Got it. Thanks everyone.
[11:10] Maya Patel: Thanks all, we'll follow up with the materials and set the benchmark start time.
[11:15] Dr. Sarah Lee: Bye.
[11:17] End of call

Notes on transcript quality: occasional transcription errors (e.g., 'tokemization' vs tokenization) and speaker interruptions. Some proper nouns may be slightly off.
